title: Bound Pair
experiment: Interference of bound pairs: the superconducting flux period h/2e (Little–Parks 1962)
intro: Two particles on one ring, tied together by a spring (the valley along the dashed diagonal: they stay close). As in 9-4 the square is the pair: across is particle 1, down is particle 2, and portals make it a torus. The pair runs along the diagonal into a wall, which it passes or bounces off as a whole, half the time each. The two halves go round the ring in opposite directions and meet at the wall again: the loop mirror of 9-1, for a pair. Find the flux that lets the pair through.
goal: Set the flux Φ through the ring so that, when the world looks at t = 28, the pair is past the wall (green) rather than back where it started (red). The answer for one particle (9-1) was Φ₀/4.

physics.point: Both particles go round the flux together, so the pair picks up twice the Aharonov–Bohm phase of one particle: its response repeats every half flux quantum, h/2e, and the window opens at Φ₀/8 instead of Φ₀/4.

idea: In 1962 Little and Parks measured the critical temperature of a thin superconducting cylinder in a magnetic field and found it oscillating with period h/2e in the enclosed flux. Every interference effect of a superconducting ring, including the SQUID magnetometer, repeats every h/2e, not h/e: the particles going round are bound pairs of electrons, each pair carrying charge 2e.

Here the pair is two particles held together by a spring. The wall splits the pair as a whole (the spring is stiff enough that the wall does not break it). Each half goes round the ring, and with both particles each picking up the phase θ = 2πΦ/Φ₀ per lap, a half picks up 2θ; the two halves, going opposite ways, differ by 4θ.
So the pair's loop mirror opens at 4θ = π, Φ = Φ₀/8, and at Φ₀/4, the window of a single particle, it is a perfect mirror again.
maths: The spring is V = ω²u²/2 in the coordinate u = (x₁ − x₂)/√2 across the diagonal, with ω = 2: the bound ground state is a Gaussian of width 1/√(2ω) = 0.5 across the diagonal, which is how the pair is launched. Its first excitation costs ω = 2, more than the wall can supply, so the pair stays bound. Each particle moves at speed 2; the walls (height 4.5 at x₁ = 20 and x₂ = 20) split the pair about 45/50.
One lap along the diagonal of the torus is 40√2 ≈ 57 long, about 20 time units. Measured at t = 28 (target / mine):
The response repeats every Φ₀/4 here, half the period of 9-1, because a pair of two charges winds the flux twice.
try: Flux 0.25, the single-particle answer: the pair comes back to the mine.
Watch the diagonal valley: the pair never leaves it.
